Transfer question: Which apparent freedoms disappear once second-order or higher equations are restored?

Title: Directions without a ruler
Mental picture: If only the direction of an arrow matters, stretching the arrow should not create a new object. Homogeneous coordinates make that decision explicit.
Shared structure: Projective space quotients nonzero vectors by common nonzero scaling.
Limits: Independent rescaling of individual coordinates changes the projective point; only one common factor is discarded. Projective invariance is stronger than scale invariance alone.
Transfer question: Which numerical differences are only artifacts of the chosen representative?
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Symmetry and invariance

Title: A lens made of monomials
Mental picture: A curved relation can become a flat condition after a lens reports products and powers as new coordinates. The lens adds coordinates without inventing independent degrees of freedom.
Shared structure: Veronese and Segre embeddings turn prescribed polynomial or rank-one structure into projective coordinates with algebraic relations.
Limits: More coordinates do not make the image fill the ambient space; relations such as vanishing minors still constrain it.
Transfer question: Can a nonlinear equation become linear after choosing richer observables?

Title: The intersection ledger
Mental picture: As curves move, two visible crossings may merge into a tangency or disappear toward infinity. A projective ledger counts multiplicities so the total remains balanced.
Shared structure: Bézout counts projective curve intersections with multiplicity when no component is shared.
Limits: Real visible intersections alone need not achieve the total; the theorem uses an algebraically closed field, projective points and no common component.
Transfer question: Which missing intersections are hidden by multiplicity, nonreal roots, or a point at infinity?

Title: A budget for allowed poles
Mental picture: Give a function permission to have poles at selected points, with specified maximum orders. Riemann–Roch counts how much freedom those permissions buy.
Shared structure: A divisor imposes local valuation bounds; the space L(D) has dimension controlled by degree, genus and a dual correction.
Limits: Permissions at different points interact globally; degree alone determines the answer only after the correction term vanishes.
Transfer question: When does adding one local allowance create one genuinely new global degree of freedom?

Title: Keeping witnesses at home
Mental picture: A smaller community can answer every question about its own members exactly as the larger community does if every existential question already has a suitable witness inside.
Shared structure: Tarski–Vaught characterizes elementary substructures through witness closure.
Limits: The questions must be first-order and use parameters from the smaller structure; the criterion does not preserve arbitrary external properties or cardinalities.
Transfer question: What witnesses must be added before a selected subset becomes logically self-sufficient?

Title: Compatible pieces of a complete answer
Mental picture: Every small collection of requirements can be satisfied. Compactness explains when all those partial successes can be assembled into one complete mathematical answer.
Shared structure: Logical compactness and compact type spaces convert finite consistency into global realizability or a complete consistent type.
Limits: This does not say one fixed finite model satisfies everything, nor that arbitrary non-first-order constraints obey compactness. Type realization may require extending the original model.
Transfer question: What exactly are the finite compatibility conditions, and in which space should their common solution live?

Title: The average as a moving reference point
Mental picture: Imagine tracking a pack of runners by measuring everyone's speed relative to the pack's average. The shared reference removes common motion and makes each runner's relative gain visible.
Shared structure: Subtracting a weighted mean creates centered quantities whose weighted sum is zero. This cancellation can preserve a normalization or reveal fluctuations around a collective reference.
Limits: The picture does not say that every average is a physical moving object. The weights must be normalized, and in replicator dynamics the weights themselves evolve; plain unweighted subtraction would not preserve the same population balance.
Transfer question: When a formula subtracts a mean, which weighted total is thereby forced to vanish?

Title: An energy ledger with a boundary
Mental picture: Picture a storehouse with an inventory, deliveries through its doors, and goods consumed inside. Any change in the inventory must be explained by those flows and internal transactions.
Shared structure: A local balance has a storage derivative, a divergence of flux, and a source or sink. Integrating over a region turns the divergence into a boundary contribution.
Limits: The conserved or balanced quantity must be specified: probability is not energy, and a source term may move a quantity into another subsystem rather than destroy it. Boundary conditions determine whether a subsystem's total stays constant.
Transfer question: What is stored, what can cross the boundary, and what internal term changes the account?
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Boundary and interior

Title: Stretching clay while preserving its volume
Mental picture: A lump of ideal incompressible clay can become long and thin without losing volume. Looking only at its longest direction could wrongly suggest that the whole lump has grown.
Shared structure: Products of local expansion factors control volume. Expansion in one direction can be exactly offset by contraction in another, while individual trajectories separate.
Limits: Phase space is a space of states, not literal material clay. A single positive directional exponent does not determine total volume change or prove every definition of chaos. The one-dimensional exponent entry describes only one direction at a time.
Transfer question: Does the system conserve a product of directional scale factors even while some individual factors grow?
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Scaling and homogeneity

Title: Several maps of the same journey
Mental picture: A route can look curved on one map and simple on another. To describe the same journey, every location and every step must translate consistently between the maps.
Shared structure: A coordinate transformation is useful when it conjugates the evolution or preserves a specified structure. Different kinds of coordinate change preserve different amounts of information.
Limits: A topological map need not preserve lengths, angles, derivative rates or smoothness. A symplectic map preserves a stronger geometric structure. Sharing a drawing or a qualitative resemblance is not enough to establish any of these relations.
Transfer question: Exactly which property must your change of coordinates preserve for the simplification to be legitimate?
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Title: Labeling a landscape by its slopes
Mental picture: Instead of identifying a hillside by location, imagine identifying a tangent plane by its slope and intercept. The description changes from where you stand to which supporting tilt you select.
Shared structure: Legendre-type transforms exchange variables with conjugate derivatives. When the derivative map is invertible, the slope can replace the original coordinate as an independent variable.
Limits: A slope may correspond to several points or no point, so a global inverse is not automatic. Convex conjugation, a regular mechanical Legendre transform and thermodynamic sign conventions have distinct hypotheses.
Transfer question: Which variable is becoming a slope label, and what condition makes that exchange reversible?

Title: Replacing a crowd by one representative neighbor
Mental picture: To understand a large crowd, imagine replacing every neighbor by an identical representative with the crowd's average behavior. Then check whether the representative's response reproduces the average you assumed.
Shared structure: A mean-field closure replaces fluctuating interacting quantities by a common expectation, producing a self-consistency equation. This is an approximation unless the omitted dependence is controlled.
Limits: The average response to a nonlinear input need not equal the response to the average input. Correlations and fluctuations can matter most near a transition, precisely where the representative-neighbor shortcut is tempting.
Transfer question: What terms are lost when you move an average inside a nonlinear function?

Title: An orchestra of independent modes
Mental picture: A complicated sound can be understood as notes that each follow a simpler rule. The right coordinates let you listen to one note at a time and then reconstruct the whole performance.
Shared structure: A suitable spectral decomposition separates a linear evolution into modes with simple individual behavior. Reconstruction sums their contributions with their original coefficients.
Limits: A nonlinear system generally couples its modes. Not every operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis, and continuous spectra are not always discrete lists of notes. Floquet factors need not be orthogonal or unitary.
Transfer question: Which operator is being simplified, and in which basis or spectral representation does its evolution separate?

Title: Clock hands that add before their lengths are measured
Mental picture: Imagine each contribution as a rotating clock hand. Hands pointing the same way reinforce one another; hands pointing opposite ways can cancel even when each is individually long.
Shared structure: Complex phases encode direction in a two-dimensional amplitude plane. Linear sums combine amplitudes before a magnitude or squared magnitude is taken.
Limits: Quantum amplitudes, classical oscillations and characteristic functions have different meanings. Squaring a sum produces interference terms; summing probabilities directly is a different operation. Angular frequency and cycles-frequency conventions must be translated carefully.
Transfer question: Are you adding signed or complex amplitudes first, or averaging nonnegative probabilities directly?

Title: Orthogonal shadows with a fixed total budget
Mental picture: Project a vector onto perpendicular directions and measure the squared length of each shadow. The shadow budgets add back to the original squared length when the directions cover the whole space.
Shared structure: Orthogonal decomposition makes squared norms additive. In a projective quantum measurement, this geometric partition becomes the probability normalization.
Limits: Ordinary visual shadows need not be orthogonal projections, and quantum probabilities are not classical hidden lengths of simultaneously possessed outcomes. Nonorthogonal vectors do not satisfy the same simple sum rule.
Transfer question: What orthogonality or completeness condition makes the total squared budget add up?

Title: Different recipes that pass the same tests
Mental picture: Two recipes can use different ingredient lists yet give identical results on every test available to an observer. The observer needs a description of the test predictions, which may not recover the original recipe.
Shared structure: A density matrix compresses a mixture preparation into its linear measurement statistics. Distinct pure-state mixtures can represent the same positive trace-one matrix.
Limits: The analogy concerns equality of all quantum measurement predictions, not approximate similarity on a few tests. A statistical mixture differs from a coherent superposition, which may contain interference absent from the mixture.
Transfer question: Does your representation preserve everything observable while intentionally forgetting how the object was prepared?

Title: Keeping a complete summary of the part you can observe
Mental picture: Imagine receiving a report about one department of a larger organization. A good summary should reproduce every statistic involving that department while omitting details that only matter to the rest.
Shared structure: Marginalization and partial trace preserve the pairing with observables restricted to a subsystem. Conditioning is a different operation that incorporates an observed outcome.
Limits: Discarding a subsystem and conditioning on a measured result are not interchangeable. An entangled pure joint state can yield a mixed reduced state without a classical mixture of hidden local pure states.
Transfer question: Are you forgetting an unobserved component or updating after learning an outcome?

Title: Finding the paired voices in a duet
Mental picture: A recording with two channels can be reorganized into pairs of patterns that belong together. The pair strengths tell you how many independent couplings are needed to reconstruct the joint performance.
Shared structure: A singular-value decomposition of bipartite amplitudes yields the Schmidt decomposition. Squared Schmidt coefficients become the eigenvalue weights of either reduced state.
Limits: The quantum version applies to bipartite pure states in this form. Classical correlated signals and quantum entanglement are different notions; a generic mixed quantum state has no single Schmidt decomposition of this kind.
Transfer question: Can a coupled object be understood through matched orthogonal pairs, and what do their weights reveal?

Title: The natural wobble reveals the response to a gentle push
Mental picture: Before pushing a system, watch how it fluctuates on its own. In thermal equilibrium, the size and correlation of those fluctuations can predict how its average changes under a small bias.
Shared structure: Differentiating normalized exponential weights produces cumulants and covariances. This relates equilibrium fluctuations to response coefficients under explicit ensemble assumptions.
Limits: This is an equilibrium relationship with the specified coupling and differentiability assumptions. A far-from-equilibrium system or noncommuting quantum observables need a different response theory; arbitrary noisy motion does not automatically reveal susceptibility.
Transfer question: Which parameter biases the weights, and which covariance appears when you differentiate the resulting average?

Title: Balancing low cost against room to move
Mental picture: Choosing a campsite involves more than finding the lowest point: a broad comfortable region may offer many more possible places to settle than one exceptionally low but tiny spot. A statistical system similarly balances energy with multiplicity.
Shared structure: Free energy combines mean energy and an entropy term. Exponential weights and log partition functions encode this balance and become sharp optimization in an appropriate low-temperature limit.
Limits: The measure defining how many possibilities exist must be fixed. A physically broad region is not automatically more probable without its energy and measure, and zero-temperature limits can be singular or have multiple minimizers.
Transfer question: Where does the formula trade a good score against the number or diversity of ways to achieve it?

Title: Changing the room-occupancy rule changes the average
Mental picture: Consider a collection of rooms. One rule permits any number of occupants in each room; another permits at most one. Even with the same price per occupant, the possible occupancy counts lead to different averages.
Shared structure: A single-mode partition sum depends on its allowed occupancy set. A geometric series and a two-term Bernoulli sum produce different normalization and mean formulas.
Limits: Quantum modes are not ordinary rooms containing distinguishable people. The analogy isolates occupation counting and does not explain spin-statistics or particle indistinguishability by itself.
Transfer question: Before averaging, what are the allowed counts or configurations being summed over?

Title: Tiles that prefer to match their neighbors
Mental picture: Imagine tiles that can show either of two colors and gain a local benefit when neighboring colors match. No tile reads the whole board, yet local interactions can create large regions of shared color.
Shared structure: Pairwise interactions on a graph create a global energy function and a correlated Gibbs distribution. Symmetries of the interaction can organize multiple collective states.
Limits: The equilibrium Gibbs model is not itself a rule for how tiles update in time. Phase transitions require an appropriate large-system limit, and finite boards retain fluctuating probabilities rather than one compulsory global arrangement.
Transfer question: How does a sum of local pairwise preferences constrain the global configurations?

Title: A bowl that splits into two valleys
Mental picture: Start with a bowl whose lowest point is in the center. As a control parameter changes, the center can rise and two equally low valleys can form on either side.
Shared structure: An even quartic potential changes its stationary points when its quadratic coefficient changes sign. Gradient flow then exhibits a supercritical pitchfork in the symmetric scalar model.
Limits: Not every transition follows a quartic model, and noise or symmetry-breaking terms can change the picture. A stationary point must be checked for stability; the existence of two wells does not by itself specify which one is reached.
Transfer question: Which symmetry forces branches to come in pairs, and which coefficient changes their stability?

Title: Walking downhill or walking along a contour
Mental picture: On a contour map, one direction descends as quickly as possible, while a perpendicular direction can follow the same elevation. The same landscape can therefore organize very different motion rules.
Shared structure: Gradient descent follows a negative gradient and dissipates its objective. Canonical Hamiltonian motion applies an antisymmetric rotation J to the energy gradient and preserves the energy when it has no explicit time dependence.
Limits: A finite gradient-descent step can overshoot, and arbitrary numerical Hamiltonian steps need not preserve energy. The contour picture is local in canonical coordinates and does not identify conserved energy with conserved phase volume.
Transfer question: Does the evolution point across the level sets, along them, or contain both kinds of motion?

Title: A gauge that can only fall
Mental picture: Suppose a machine carries a gauge that never rises while it runs. Instead of predicting every moving part, use the gauge and the conditions for its needle to stop falling to identify what motion can persist.
Shared structure: A Lyapunov function converts dynamics into a scalar monotonicity statement. LaSalle refines a nonstrict decrease condition by finding the invariant part of the zero-decrease set.
Limits: A decreasing gauge alone need not imply convergence to one state. The gauge must control the relevant state, and compactness, coercivity or invariant-set assumptions determine what stronger conclusion is justified.
Transfer question: When the gauge stops falling momentarily, can the system remain in that set forever?
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Conservation and balance

Title: A strobe light turns a dance into steps
Mental picture: A continuous dance can be studied by looking only once each cycle or whenever the dancer crosses a marked line. Repeating motion becomes a stationary pattern in the sampled sequence.
Shared structure: A return map converts selected continuous-time crossings into discrete evolution. For periodic linear coefficients, the one-period monodromy matrix similarly summarizes growth across cycles.
Limits: Sampling can miss motion or create misleading apparent periods. A Poincaré section needs transversality and actual returns, while Floquet sampling uses a prescribed coefficient period; they are related constructions with different hypotheses.
Transfer question: What single return or period operator captures the part of continuous motion you care about?

Title: Zooming into a bend in the road
Mental picture: A curved road looks almost straight through a sufficiently small window. Near a special junction, however, even a tiny bend can decide which routes exist, so the straight approximation may lose crucial information.
Shared structure: First derivatives control local approximation, but qualitative dynamical conclusions require conditions such as hyperbolicity. At a bifurcation, the decisive linear condition fails and higher-order terms matter.
Limits: Small numerical error in a local approximation does not automatically preserve long-term dynamics. A topological conjugacy also need not preserve actual distances or rates.
Transfer question: Is the first derivative decisive here, or has it become degenerate exactly where the behavior changes?

Title: Small errors multiply, their logarithms add
Mental picture: Imagine each stage of a process stretching or shrinking a tiny error by a different factor. To understand the whole chain, add the logarithms of the factors and then look at their average.
Shared structure: Derivatives of iterates multiply by the chain rule. A logarithmic time average therefore measures exponential sensitivity and corresponds to a geometric mean of local multipliers.
Limits: A local infinitesimal error model may fail once the error becomes large. Zero derivatives, absent limits and multidimensional directional effects need care; positive sensitivity alone is not every possible definition of chaos.
Transfer question: Is the natural average arithmetic because contributions add, or geometric because changes multiply?

Title: Averaging away motion to expose what stays fixed
Mental picture: Imagine making many transformed copies of a measurement and averaging them. Components that keep moving through opposite directions cancel, while components unchanged by every step remain.
Shared structure: Cesàro averaging of unitary iterates projects onto invariant vectors. In measure-preserving dynamics, related time averages identify the information that survives the evolution.
Limits: Norm convergence and almost-everywhere convergence are different claims with different hypotheses. Ergodicity is needed to reduce all invariant information to one constant space average, and exceptional trajectories can remain.
Transfer question: After many transformations are averaged, what invariant subspace or invariant information is left?

Title: A finite hall that cannot keep admitting disjoint crowds
Mental picture: Imagine a hall of fixed capacity and a crowd rearrangement that preserves every group's size. A positive-size group cannot move forever into completely new disjoint parts of the hall.
Shared structure: Finite measure and measure preservation rule out a positive-measure wandering set. This gives recurrence for almost every point in a measurable region.
Limits: The theorem does not bound waiting time or promise an exact return to a single point. Finite total measure is essential, and recurrence is not the same as mixing or equilibration.
Transfer question: Which finite preserved quantity prevents the system from wandering into disjoint new regions forever?

Title: Several people adjusting the same machine
Mental picture: Several people each control one dial and adjust it to improve their own reading. A settled configuration means no person wants to change their dial alone; it need not be best for the group.
Shared structure: Mutual best response is a coordinate-wise incentive condition. A shared potential is an additional structure that can turn those separate improvements into monotone progress of one scalar.
Limits: Separate objectives can create cycles, and equilibrium need not be socially optimal. Even a common potential can have several local optima, and the finite-game termination argument applies to strict improvements over finitely many profiles.
Transfer question: Do all local improvements move one shared quantity in the same direction, or can the incentives conflict?

Title: A traffic light as a correlated plan
Mental picture: Two drivers can flip independent coins about who goes first, or follow a shared light that gives complementary recommendations. Coordination changes the joint outcome distribution even when each driver's overall chance of going is the same.
Shared structure: A joint distribution contains dependence that is absent from a product of independent strategies. Incentive constraints differ depending on whether a deviation is chosen before or after observing a private recommendation.
Limits: The analogy assumes the payoffs make obedience sensible; merely adding a shared signal does not create an equilibrium. Publicly revealing more information can change the incentive constraints.
Transfer question: What does each participant know at the moment they are allowed to choose a deviation?
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Information and uncertainty

Title: The running tab on a crowded resource
Mental picture: A venue records the cost of admitting the first guest, then the next, and so on. The extra line on the tab when one guest joins is the cost that guest now faces.
Shared structure: Discrete summation and continuous integration construct a potential whose difference or derivative recovers marginal congestion cost.
Limits: The potential is generally not the total cost paid by all users. Unweighted finite congestion games and nonatomic flows require different formulas; weighted players need further assumptions.
Transfer question: Can you integrate or sum a marginal rule to obtain one potential that tracks every allowed local change?

Title: Giving credit by averaging arrival orders
Mental picture: Imagine a team forming one person at a time. Each arrival receives credit for the extra result made possible at that moment, and fairness is assessed by averaging over every possible arrival order.
Shared structure: Shapley allocation averages marginal contributions under a uniform random permutation. In each permutation those marginal contributions telescope to the total coalition worth.
Limits: The fairness properties depend on the chosen coalition-worth model and axioms. This allocation is not automatically a causal contribution estimate or a stable outcome in the cooperative core.
Transfer question: Would changing the order of combination change an item's marginal contribution, and should those orders be averaged?

Title: An invoice for the alternatives you displace
Mental picture: A participant joins a shared allocation and changes what everyone else can obtain. An externality invoice asks how much worse the others' best attainable outcome becomes because of that participant's selected outcome.
Shared structure: VCG pivot payments compare a counterfactual optimum for the other participants with their value in the chosen total-welfare optimum.
Limits: A counterfactual externality payment is not generally equal to one Lagrange multiplier. Truthfulness relies on the valuation and utility assumptions and does not imply that collected payments cover costs or balance a budget.
Transfer question: Is the relevant price a local derivative, an allocation threshold, or a finite counterfactual difference?

Title: Sharing gains above a disagreement floor
Mental picture: Before dividing a surplus, draw each person's fallback level as a floor. A balanced agreement compares improvements above those floors rather than comparing final numbers in isolation.
Shared structure: The Nash product maximizes a product of positive gains, equivalently their geometric mean or the sum of their logarithms, over a feasible utility set.
Limits: The fallback levels and feasible utility set are part of the model. Equal gains follow only in suitable symmetric cases; bargaining axioms do not make unlike utilities directly comparable by arbitrary rescaling.
Transfer question: What is the meaningful baseline, and should fairness compare absolute outcomes or improvements above it?

Title: A translator that preserves the answer
Mental picture: An unfamiliar puzzle can be translated into a familiar puzzle if every yes-answer and every no-answer survive the translation. Solving the translated version then solves the original.
Shared structure: A many-one reduction is a total transformation preserving language membership. A complexity reduction must additionally control the time and output size of the translation.
Limits: A resemblance between puzzles is not a reduction. Correctness must work in both answer directions for all inputs, and a slow or exponentially expanding translator can invalidate the intended complexity conclusion.
Transfer question: What explicit translation preserves the answer, and how much computational work does the translation itself hide?

Title: One interpreter, many recipes
Mental picture: A cook can follow many recipes without becoming a different cook for each dish. A fixed interpreter likewise changes behavior by reading a different program description.
Shared structure: Universal computation treats programs as data. A fixed interpreter can also translate description languages with a constant additional program-length cost under an optimal encoding.
Limits: A recipe can fail to finish, and a universal simulator may be much slower than a specialized implementation. Constant description overhead does not imply constant runtime overhead.
Transfer question: Which cost belongs to the reusable interpreter, and which cost grows with the particular description or execution?

Title: An instruction card that reverses its own prediction
Mental picture: Suppose a perfect predictor announces whether an instruction card will finish. Write a card that loops if predicted to finish and finishes if predicted to loop, then ask about that card itself.
Shared structure: Diagonal self-reference constructs behavior that disagrees with a purported universal predictor on its own encoded description.
Limits: The construction assumes a total correct predictor for all programs; it does not show that every particular program is mysterious. Cardinality diagonalization and effective computability diagonalization also use different formal settings.
Transfer question: Can a purported universal description be fed back into a construction designed to disagree with it?

Title: Checking an itinerary versus finding one
Mental picture: It can be easy to check a supplied itinerary against local travel rules even when searching for a valid itinerary is difficult. The itinerary is a witness, and the checker verifies it step by step.
Shared structure: NP separates a polynomial-size certificate from a polynomial-time verifier. Cook–Levin encodes a bounded accepting computation using local consistency constraints.
Limits: Easy verification is not a proof that search is hard, and not every true claim has a polynomial-size witness. A no-instance must reject every permitted witness, not merely a few attempted itineraries.
Transfer question: What would a short independently checkable certificate look like, and can all its local checks be performed efficiently?

Title: Exploring a maze while reusing the same notes
Mental picture: An explorer may visit a huge number of routes while carrying only a small notebook. They erase and reuse pages after each branch instead of storing every attempted route at once.
Shared structure: Space complexity measures simultaneously stored information, while time counts all steps. Savitch's midpoint recursion trades repeated work for bounded reusable workspace.
Limits: The implicit maze may be exponentially larger than its compact description. Saving memory can require enormous extra time; a space bound should not be presented as an efficiency guarantee for runtime.
Transfer question: Which information must remain simultaneously available, and which can be recomputed or discarded between branches?

Title: Twenty questions and the cost of sorting
Mental picture: Each yes-or-no question divides the remaining possibilities into at most two groups. To identify one possibility among many, a question tree needs enough leaves, regardless of how clever its questions sound.
Shared structure: A binary decision tree of depth d has at most 2^d leaves. Distinguishing n! possible orders therefore requires at least log₂(n!) comparisons in the worst case.
Limits: An arbitrary yes-or-no question and a comparison between two keys have different restrictions. Worst-case depth, average code length and self-information are related quantities but are not interchangeable bounds.
Transfer question: How many distinguishable outcomes must the decision process have, and how much branching can one step supply?

Title: A machine with finitely many memory badges
Mental picture: A clerk stamps each processed prefix with one of finitely many badges. If two prefixes receive the same badge, the clerk must respond identically to every identical continuation.
Shared structure: A deterministic automaton state summarizes future acceptance behavior. Myhill–Nerode classes give the minimal possible summaries, and repeated states produce pumpable loops.
Limits: The machine must have a fixed finite state set independent of input length. The pumping property is a necessary consequence of regularity, while the finite-index Myhill–Nerode criterion is an exact characterization.
Transfer question: Which distinctions about the past can ever affect the future, and how many such distinctions must the system remember?

Title: Too many objects for too few short labels
Mental picture: A warehouse has more distinct items than available short labels. Some items must receive longer labels no matter how ingenious the labeling scheme is.
Shared structure: Counting possible descriptions against possible objects proves incompressibility. This can establish that hard-to-describe objects exist without identifying a particular one efficiently.
Limits: An existence-by-counting argument does not automatically give an explicit hard example or an algorithm for certifying shortest descriptions. The description language and the object family must be fixed before counting.
Transfer question: Can a simple count of available descriptions prove that some objects need more structure or length?

Title: Fresh independent checks and a majority decision
Mental picture: Repeat a fallible check using fresh independent randomness each time. If each check is reliably better than guessing, a majority decision becomes much more dependable as the number of checks grows.
Shared structure: Correctness indicators are bounded independent variables. Their arithmetic mean concentrates around its expectation, separating it from the majority threshold.
Limits: Repeated checks sharing the same systematic failure may be highly correlated and gain little reliability. The bound uses per-input guarantees and fresh independent runs, not an assumption that most problem instances are easy.
Transfer question: Where does independence enter, and is the average separated from the decision threshold by a fixed margin?

Title: Freezing one lucky schedule that passes every test
Mental picture: Randomly choose a schedule for a whole collection of tests. If the probability of any test failing is less than one, some fixed schedule must pass them all, even if finding it is difficult.
Shared structure: A union bound converts small individual failure probabilities into the existence of one globally successful choice. Hardwiring that choice changes a randomized object into a nonuniform deterministic one.
Limits: The argument proves existence, not an efficient uniform construction of the schedule. In Adleman's theorem the successful seed may depend on input length; hardwiring different seeds is precisely the nonuniform feature.
Transfer question: Can you make every local failure probability small enough that one global choice must satisfy all constraints?
